newsitem.title: BULGARIA: FOCUS - Bulgaria ready for currency board -- finmin.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bulgaria ready for currency board -- finmin.

text.p: Bulgaria has met most of the conditions to prepare implementation of a fixed exchange rate regime agreed with the International Monetary Fund last month, Finance Minister Svetoslav Gavriiski said on Wednesday.

"The caretaker government will prepare by the end of this week a report on completion of the prior actions to be presented to the IMF board. I see no serious obstacles for a favourable decision," Gavriiski said after a cabinet meeting.

Bulgaria pledged to introduce a fixed exchange rate system known as the currency board in June to restore confidence in its collapsing financial system. The pledge came under a $510 million 14-month IMF standby accord agreed last month.
The IMF board is expected to review the cabinet's preparations for the currency board and consider disbursing the first tranche of the standby on April 11, said Gavriiski.
He predicted macroeconomic stabilisation, falling inflation and interest rates and rising wages in the first months after the introduction of the system.
As part of the preparations the caretaker government has adopted a draft 1997 budget frame, which must be approved by the new government and parliament to be formed after April 19 general elections.
"The budget parameters will be adjusted after the lev is fixed to a foreign currency at the market rate at the time of introduction of the currency board," said Gavriiski.
The new parliament will decide on whether to peg the lev to the dollar or the mark.

Under the budget frame drafted jointly with the IMF, annual inflation this year is seen at 700 percent, mainly due to the galloping 392 percent cumulative inflation for the first two months of this year, said Gavriiski.
Monthly inflation in March was expected at 10 percent, he said. Inflation subsided mainly due to the strengthening of the lev in the past month, which lowered prices on imported goods.
The lev has remained steady at around 1,600 levs to the dollar since March 10, after tumbling in February to a record low of 3,000 to the dollar.

"The interim government persuaded banks to invest in government securities, which prompted them to sell dollars on the domestic market and boosted budget revenues," said Gavriiski. Central bank reserves rose by $100 million in March to $550 million, he added.
The government and commercial banks did not borrow funds from the central bank in March, he said. Limiting central bank lending is a major currency board requirement.
The system would require levs in circulation to be matched by central bank reserves, severely curbing the financial powers of the government and the central bank and preventing the printing of money.
The finance ministry has set up a tax administration unit to boost revenue, another IMF recommendation.

Under a currency board, annual interest rates are expected to be set by the market and to fall to between 20 and 30 percent immediately after its introduction and to 10 percent by year-end, he said. The annual interest rate is currently set by the central bank at 216 percent.
Bulgaria must also stabilise its troubled banks before introduction of the currency board.
The interim cabinet has drafted amendments to two banking laws and the bankruptcy law, which need to be passed by the next parliament to make the board operational.

On Monday the cabinet launched a $50 million stabilisation plan for the state Biochim bank in line with pledges to the IMF. It has invited major foreign banks to tender for management of ailing local banks.
In line with IMF recommendations the government raised grain prices to $160 per tonne and announced that farm produce prices will be liberalised shortly.

Average state monthly wages are expected to rise from current $30 to up to $75 in the next few months as the economy stabilises, said Gavriiski, adding that the government has envisaged privatisation income of up to $350 million this year. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
